title: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study
abstract: We present a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) that compares a deterministic template baseline to a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using a deterministic validator. Under the frozen confirmatory semantics (shared_initial_candidate per pair) all confirmatory episodes completed: baseline = 120/120 verifier passes; guarded (gpt‑5‑mini, seed_0) = 120/120 verifier passes. Paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We publish the exact execution and analysis artifacts and SHA‑256 fingerprints required to reproduce the run (see execution/execution_manifest.json in the artifact bundle). Using the archived traces we diagnose why the paired outcome is uninformative about independent generative reliability (preregistered shared_initial_candidate design, template‑tight task synthesis, and validator–task coupling) and we provide artifact‑grounded runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversification, and expanded task heterogeneity) to yield informative, reproducible comparisons for operational NetOps questions. The immutable initial master prompt is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

sections.introduction:
Automating network operations (NetOps) by translating high‑level human intent into device configuration is an operational imperative: it promises faster change cycles and lower human error rates, but raises correctness and safety questions because device commands have immediate and system‑wide semantic effects (reachability, access control, transient safety during multi‑step changes). Deterministic validators that compute the semantic effect of a proposed configuration (reachability, ACL equivalence, routing invariants, and transient constraints) are standard tools in network verification and pre‑deployment validation [doi:10.1145/3603269.3604866].

We preregistered a hypothesis‑driven study (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) to compare a deterministic template baseline against a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on operational intent→configuration tasks. The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (per‑task binary verifier pass, averaged across N = 120 paired tasks). All elements of the execution chain were frozen prior to model calls and archived (execution/execution_manifest.json). The run used a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) to produce objective pass/fail judgments and full validator traces (execution/scoring/*.json). The initial master prompt that governed autonomous orchestration is archived immutably (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

This paper (i) reports the preregistered confirmatory outcome with complete artifact pointers and cryptographic fingerprints, (ii) uses the archived traces to explain why the confirmatory contrast is degenerate under the preregistered shared_candidate semantics, and (iii) documents concrete, artifact‑anchored experimental adjustments that preserve reproducibility while enabling informative inference about independent generative reliability.
sections.related_work:
Verifier‑grounded NetOps evaluation and intent translation. Offline network semantics analyzers (Batfish and successors) are widely used to validate configuration changes before deployment; operational experience shows that semantics checking can prevent outages caused by configuration mistakes [doi:10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Recent LLM→NetOps literature focuses on intent translation, generate–validate–repair loops, and guarded agentic pipelines; authors argue that token/fluency metrics are poor proxies for operational correctness and that deterministic semantic validators are essential for trustworthy NetOps automation (examples and surveys are summarized in the archived literature corpus included with the run [https://doi.org/10.23919/cnsm62983.2024.10814407, https://doi.org/10.1002/nem.70029]).

Methodological gap. Prior evaluations commonly mix independent generation, iterative repair, and ad‑hoc validator use without preregistered estimands or exhaustive artifact publication. This makes it difficult to know whether reported improvements reflect generator reliability, repair logic, validator sensitivity, or evaluation design choices. Our contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑oriented: a frozen, preregistered paired design with deterministic validator traces and exhaustive SHA‑256 artifact manifests to allow byte‑for‑byte re‑execution and immediate, artifact‑grounded diagnosis.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The full preregistration CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1 (SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) defined the confirmatory estimand, N = 120 tasks (40 per topology class: edge, datacenter, multi‑AS), paired design, deterministic validator, generation semantics, seeds, stopping rules, exclusion and missingness policies, and analysis plan (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The preregistered plan and the execution manifest are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json). The declared model used by the run is recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini; SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

Task generation and template design. Tasks were synthesized programmatically from a deterministic template bank using deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (generator_version 5.0). Each task manifest entry (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 ee55625286dcd27c0a4977043e890054f6456771c202b33c5c9c767233e6568a) encodes: initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit required_sequence (the minimal safe command sequence), workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), allowed_touched_fields, and annotated difficulty (changed_interface_count, transient_rule_count). Representative tasks and seeds are available in the artifact_examples section of the bundle (e.g., task‑000001 through task‑000006). The template bank intentionally encodes precise operational constraints (atomic MTU update patterns, make‑before‑break uplink switchover, rolling VLAN migrations) so the validator has unambiguous rules to check.

Generation semantics, adapter, and scoring. The run used adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the provider adapter 'openai_responses' to dispatch generation calls. The preregistered confirmatory generation semantics was shared_initial_candidate: the pipeline generated one canonical candidate per pair (shared_initial) and then submitted that identical candidate for both baseline and guarded scoring episodes; the shared candidates are archived at execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt (representative SHA‑256s: task‑000001 shared SHA‑256 8f38c8becd7e1e36..., task‑000003 shared SHA‑256 f7f4db249ecb...). Candidate scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0) under scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation; each scoring episode produced a structured JSON trace (execution/scoring/*.json) containing parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, validator final_state and any violation codes. Representative scoring JSONs include execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57f...), execution/scoring/task-000003-guarded.json (SHA‑256 dad1cf4cfd80b4cc...), and analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA‑256 9c77c96f37c4b6ff...).

Statistical analysis and reproducibility specifics. The confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1. Per the preregistration we computed a 95% bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) on the paired difference and applied the exact McNemar two‑sided test for discordant pairs. All analysis scripts and intermediate files (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 9f25790c..., analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg SHA‑256 ae5b8e0c...) are archived to permit exact reproduction. The execution manifest contains exhaustive per‑file SHA‑256 fingerprints (execution/execution_manifest.json) so auditors can re‑run the same artifact chain deterministically.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw outcomes. The preregistered run executed in scientific_confirmatory mode. Planned_episode_count = 240 (120 pairs × 2 conditions); completed_episode_count = 240; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 120 (shared_initial generation counted once per pair); provider call traces and call_cache entries are archived (execution/provider_calls/*.json and execution/call_cache/*.json). There were no infrastructure retry events required.

Confirmatory pass counts and contingency. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the archived scoring outputs show:
- baseline_success_count = 120/120 (baseline pass rate = 1.00)
- guarded_success_count = 120/120 (gpt‑5‑mini pass rate = 1.00)
The paired contingency table is degenerate: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 9f25790c...). The primary estimate (mean of guarded_i − baseline_i) = 0.00.

Confirmatory inference (preregistered). Bootstrap (10,000 replicates, seed = 1729) on the paired difference yields a degenerate 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg SHA‑256 ae5b8e0c...). The exact McNemar two‑sided test returns p = 1.0. These computations were performed by the archived analysis executor (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 ff20bc07...). All numeric artifacts and code are included in the bundle for deterministic reexecution.

Representative validator trace diagnostic. The validator JSON trace for task‑000001 (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json; SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57f...) contains both validation_before and validation_after snapshots. Example recorded fields: parsed_command_count = 4; required_command_count = 4; observed_touched_field_count = 3; normalized_configuration equals the shared candidate; final_state enumerates interface admin, mtu, vlan values. This explicit trace shows the validator confirmed the canonical candidate satisfied the task's required_sequence and transient workflow_policies (violation_count = 0). Similar identical shared candidate SHA‑256 fingerprints appear across multiple pairs (e.g., execution/responses/task-000003-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 f7f4db249ecb...), demonstrating reuse of identical artifacts for baseline and guarded episodes under the preregistered semantics.

Contamination and exposure checks. The preregistered string‑overlap contamination heuristics were executed and recorded in analysis/contamination_summary.csv (SHA‑256 389227f0...), which contains no confirmed contamination flags under the chosen thresholds. The absence of a flag is not proof of zero exposure; full provider call traces and call_cache entries are published for independent, stronger exposure analyses by auditors.
sections.discussion:
What the confirmatory test measured—and why it is uninformative about independent generation reliability. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics deliberately generated one canonical candidate per pair and evaluated that identical artifact under both baseline and guarded scoring episodes. Deterministic validator judgments thus necessarily agree when presented the same artifact and scoring rules. The degenerate paired outcome (both conditions 120/120) is therefore arithmetically correct but substantively uninformative about whether independent draws from the LLM would satisfy validator constraints with equal probability. The archived evidence supporting this explanation includes the identical shared candidate files (execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt; representative SHA‑256s: 8f38c8be..., f7f4db24...) and the scoring JSONs that report parser counts and final_state (execution/scoring/*.json; representative SHA‑256s provided above).

Preregistered but unanswered operational question. Operators care about independent generative reliability: given independent LLM generations, what is the probability a generated candidate satisfies operational validator constraints? The archived confirmatory design did not estimate that probability because it removed generation variability by construction. We therefore recommend two artifact‑anchored modifications that preserve determinism and reproducibility while producing informative answers:
1) Independent_per_condition confirmatory sampling: reconfigure the generator adapter to produce one independent candidate per condition per pair (e.g., baseline: seed_b, guarded: seed_g), then rerun the deterministic validator. The execution harness and all scoring tools are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json) so this rerun can be executed deterministically and the resulting contingency table will reflect independent generation variability. 2) Multi‑seed confirmatory replication: produce K ≥ 3 independent seeds per condition per task and estimate per‑condition pass probability with bootstrap CIs; archived seeds and generation code allow exact replication of the random draws. Both modifications are runnable with the provided artifacts and maintain the preregistration's determinism guarantees.

Threats to validity and operational implications. Internal validity: the preregistered shared_initial design intentionally controlled generation variability and therefore cannot assess the independent generative question. Construct validity: deterministic validators faithfully enforce template constraints but may overstate real‑world reliability for broader, less templated intents. External validity: the study used a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) under one adapter and a bank of synthetic templated tasks; results do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or open‑form operational language. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency yields trivial inferential statistics that are correct but do not address the operational question of LLM robustness under independent sampling. All these threats are visible in the archived artifacts (task manifests, shared candidate files, and validator traces) and can be addressed by the artifact‑grounded reruns described above.

Practitioner guidance. For operational adoption, we recommend that evaluations (i) explicitly choose generation semantics that match the deployment decision (independent sampling when deciding generator reliability), (ii) use at least K = 3 independent seeds per condition in confirmatory comparisons to estimate pass probability with precision, (iii) diversify validators (reachability, ACL checker, emulation) and report intersection/union pass rates to limit validator–task coupling, and (iv) publish exhaustive artifacts with cryptographic fingerprints so auditors can re‑run and audit evaluation choices. The current artifact bundle already contains all required files to execute these recommended reruns deterministically (see execution/execution_manifest.json for the exhaustive per‑file manifest and SHA‑256s).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, verifier‑grounded paired experiment and released a complete artifact bundle enabling byte‑level reproduction (execution/execution_manifest.json; model configuration: execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820; master prompt: provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e...). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both the deterministic template baseline and the gpt‑5‑mini guarded condition validated on all N = 120 tasks (both 120/120). Archived evidence (shared candidate files and validator scoring traces) demonstrates that identical canonical candidates per pair and template‑tight tasks caused the degenerate paired outcome; consequently the confirmatory paired result does not provide evidence about independent LLM generative reliability in operational settings. We publish artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory execution, validator diversification, task heterogeneity expansion) that preserve reproducibility and enable informative independent comparisons that operators require for deployment decisions. All execution and analysis artifacts—including the immutable master prompt reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and the preregistration SHA‑256—are included in the submission bundle to permit exact audit and follow‑up experiments. Transparent preregistration plus exhaustive artifact publication clarifies precisely what a confirmatory test measures and accelerates corrective reruns answering operationally meaningful questions for NetOps automation.

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: programmatic templates produced narrow required_sequences and workflow_policies that favour canonical solutions and limit external generalizability to heterogeneous operational intents.

Confirmatory shared_initial semantics: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair, reducing independence between conditions and causing the degenerate paired outcome.

Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary analysis used one canonical seed per task; preregistered exploratory multi‑seed analyses (seeds_1..4) were not included in the confirmatory inference reported here.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces constraints encoded in the task templates, which can increase pass rates for template‑aligned candidates and reduce construct validity for open distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: preregistered contamination heuristics found no flags under chosen thresholds, but absence of a flag is not proof of zero exposure to related artifacts in model pretraining.

Single‑model, single‑validator run: results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded configuration and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; they do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or other validators.
